opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the Waymo Foundation Model is really about taking everything we've learned from years of driving and putting it into one large, general model that understands the world the way a driver needs to: perceiving the scene, understanding what other road users are likely to do, and reasoning about how we should act.

Historically, a lot of autonomous driving stacks were built from many specialized components, each tuned for a particular task. That works, but it becomes harder to scale as you add new cities, new weather conditions, and new kinds of vehicles. With a foundation model, you train on a huge and diverse body of data: our own fleet's driving, simulation, and broader world knowledge. You get representations that generalize much better. Then you can adapt or distill that knowledge into the models that actually run onboard, which have to be fast, efficient, and safe.

So it helps us scale in a few ways. First, generalization: when we go to a new city, a lot of what the model has learned already transfers, so we're not starting from scratch. Second, the long tail: the hard part of driving is the rare, weird situations, like unusual construction, someone doing something unexpected, or odd objects on the road. Large models with richer world knowledge are much better at handling those gracefully. Third, it powers our offboard ecosystem, not just the car. The same kind of model helps with auto-labeling, mining interesting scenarios from data, and building more realistic simulation, where agents behave like real people would. That closes the loop: better simulation lets us evaluate and improve the driver faster.

One thing I'd emphasize is that, for us, scale has to come together with safety and verifiability. A foundation model is powerful, but we still need a rigorous way to validate the behavior that ends up on the road. So a big part of the work is combining the generality of these large models with the structure and evaluation infrastructure that let us be confident in how the system behaves. That combination is really what lets us expand to more places and more people responsibly.

r002.rationale: It says the model's learning transfers to a new city, so Waymo is not starting from scratch when expanding geographically.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose giving the data-center model access to information beyond what is available as events unfold.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it, the Waymo Foundation Model is really the backbone of how we scale, and it addresses a few different problems at once.

If you step back and look at how autonomous driving systems were built historically, you had a lot of separate, hand-engineered modules: perception, prediction, planning, each with its own representations and interfaces. That worked, and it got us to a driverless product, but every new capability or new environment meant touching many pieces and re-tuning the handoffs between them. That's a very expensive way to grow.

What a foundation model gives us is a single, large model trained end-to-end on enormous amounts of our own driving data, and then specialized for the tasks we care about. The key property is that capability improves with scale, in data and in model size, and that improvement transfers across tasks. So when we expand to a new city, we're not starting from zero. The model has already seen a tremendous diversity of road geometry, weather, agents, and behaviors, and what remains is a much smaller adaptation problem rather than a re-engineering problem.

The second piece is world knowledge. Our driving data is rich, but it's still a slice of the world. By building on top of large multimodal models, like Gemini, the system brings in semantic understanding you can't easily get from driving logs alone. It knows what a school bus is, what construction workers signaling with hand gestures mean, what a temporary sign is likely telling it. That lets it reason about the long tail of rare situations in a much more general way, instead of us having to anticipate and encode each one.

The third piece is that the foundation model isn't just the driver. It also powers our simulation and evaluation. We use it to generate realistic scenarios, to model how other agents behave, and to stress-test the onboard system at a scale you could never achieve with real-world miles alone. So you get this virtuous cycle: more driving produces more data, the model gets better, the simulator gets better, and we can validate new capabilities and new geographies faster and with more confidence.

And then on the practical side, there's the question of how you get a very large model to run on a car. We train the big model offboard, and then distill it into something that fits the compute and latency constraints onboard, while preserving as much of its capability as we can. That distillation path is what lets us keep raising the ceiling of the research model without being bottlenecked by what fits in the vehicle today.

So when I talk about scaling, I mean all of that together: fewer bespoke components, a system that gets better with every mile, broad world knowledge for the rare cases, and a simulation engine that lets us prove safety before we deploy. That's what the foundation model unlocks for us.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that scaling autonomous driving means being able to handle an enormous variety of situations without having to solve each one independently. You want the experience you gain in one city to help you drive better in another city, even though the roads, the traffic patterns, and the behaviors you encounter may be different.

The foundation model gives us a way to share that learning. Perception, prediction, and planning are closely connected: understanding what you’re seeing helps you anticipate what other road users might do, and that informs how you should drive. Learning those relationships together can give us better generalization and make more effective use of the driving data we collect.

But there’s also the question of how you know the system is ready. Better models need to go hand in hand with simulation, evaluation, and careful validation. So the opportunity is both to reduce the work required to adapt to new environments and to make that expansion something we can assess rigorously.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that scaling autonomous driving is fundamentally about generalization. You can’t collect and engineer a separate solution for every situation a vehicle might encounter. You need models that can learn from a broad range of experience and apply that knowledge to new situations.

With the Waymo Foundation Model, we’re bringing together learning across driving, simulation, and understanding the world. Those capabilities reinforce each other. A better understanding of how the world behaves helps us build better simulations, and simulation lets us challenge the driving system with a much wider range of scenarios.

The opportunity is to make the system more capable while reducing the amount of work required to adapt it to new environments. But we still have to demonstrate that those improvements translate into safe driving. Generalization is what enables scale; rigorous evaluation is how we establish that we’re ready to deploy.
